abstract.p: Research at the interface of biodiversity conservation, urban forestry, and urban green space spans ecology, forestry, landscape planning, environmental management, and public health, making its intellectual structure difficult to apprehend through narrative review alone. This study maps a corpus of 3747 documents published from 2006 to 17 August 2026, retrieved from the OpenAlex API on 13 October 2026 after integrity checking and deduplication. Performance analysis, country-level collaboration networks, lexical co-occurrence on titles and abstracts (abstract coverage 82.6% after supplementation), strategic mapping, thematic evolution, co-citation, and bibliographic coupling were computed with scripts released with the article; stochastic community partitions were evaluated over 200 seeded runs. Across the complete years 2006–2025, retrieved annual output increased at a compound annual rate of 15.89%. The corpus spans 1316 journals and affiliations in 124 countries. China leads publication output, whereas Germany and the USA occupy the strongest brokerage positions in the collaboration network. Author-derived text resolves six lexical clusters (modularity = 0.442), in which health and planning vocabulary joins climate and green-infrastructure terms and carbon vocabulary joins tree and plant species, and co-citation of the 200 most cited references identifies six communities (modularity = 0.507). More than half of the corpus (54.9%) enters only through green-space terms, and removing these documents changes the lexical partition substantially; a replica of a prior green-space mapping shows that urban-forestry terms distinguish the corpus. The mapped literature is increasingly connected to climate, health, and planning agendas.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Urbanisation is among the most consequential and least reversible land transformations of the present century. Probabilistic forecasts indicate that global urban land cover could approach a threefold increase relative to its extent circa 2000, with the fastest expansion projected in regions of exceptional conservation value [1]. Scenario-based projections corroborate this trajectory across the twenty-first century [2], while complementary analyses show that the indirect displacement of natural land frequently exceeds the direct footprint of built-up expansion [3]. The biodiversity consequences are correspondingly severe: future urban growth is projected to fragment and eliminate substantial areas of terrestrial vertebrate habitat, with disproportionate encroachment upon priority conservation areas [4,5].

The ecological literature on urban biodiversity developed along a trajectory legible in its own citation record. Early syntheses established urbanisation as a distinctive driver of local extinction and of biotic homogenisation, whereby the same urban-adaptable species become widespread across cities worldwide [6,7], and the reframing of the city as an integrated social-ecological system [8] supplied the architecture within which subsequent work was situated. Global comparative analysis quantified species-density loss in cities while showing that anthropogenic rather than biogeographic variables best explain residual diversity [9], and meta-analysis established green-space area and connectivity as the dominant determinants of intra-urban variation [10]. Later work reframed urban assemblages as the outcome of hierarchically nested filters [11] and specified the questions that must be resolved if urban green spaces are to serve as conservation habitat [12], a programme resting on the earlier articulation of the ecology–planning interface [13] and on landscape-ecological synthesis [14]. Experimental intervention confirms that manipulable attributes of vegetation structure yield gains across taxa [15], private gardens and spontaneous woodlands support native and threatened species [16,17], residential tree diversity responds jointly to ecological and social determinants [18], and a recent assessment consolidates these strands [19].

A second body of work situates urban vegetation within the ecosystem-service framework. The foundational articulation of urban ecosystem services [20] preceded an empirical literature on the regulation of urban water, heat, and pollutant cycles [21], city-wide above-ground carbon storage [22], the accounting of tree-derived benefits against their costs [23], and the restoration of urban services as an intervention class [24]; the formulation of urban forests as instruments for preserving biodiversity [25] belongs to the same period. Parallel work asks whether urban forests, ecosystem services, green infrastructure, and nature-based solutions form an analytical nexus or a succession of evolving metaphors [26], while syntheses document persistent methodological heterogeneity in service assessment [27,28] and specify the environmental and health limits of tree planting as policy [29].

A third strand concerns the social distribution of urban vegetation and its relation to human health. Distributional analyses repeatedly associate canopy cover with neighbourhood affluence [30,31] and relate present-day canopy distribution to historical housing policy [32]; the generality of the luxury effect has been examined for biodiversity as well as canopy [33,34], justice considerations have been formalised within service scholarship [35], and survey evidence indicates broad support for biodiversity across culturally heterogeneous European cities [36]. Concurrently, evidence has accumulated for beneficial associations between greenspace exposure and health [37] and—critically for what follows—for a positive association between the species richness of urban greenspace and psychological well-being [38]. Mechanistic biodiversity–health frameworks have since been elaborated [39,40] and examined at fine spatial scales, where associations differ according to the vegetation attribute considered [41]. The nature-based-solutions agenda has integrated these concerns within a policy-facing framework [42,43,44], backed by adaptation evidence [45], health-impact estimates of urban-heat-island mortality and deaths potentially preventable through increased tree cover [46], and European assessments of green-infrastructure cooling [47].

This heterogeneity generates a methodological requirement: to progress beyond narrative characterisation and interrogate the field as a structured knowledge system. Bibliometric analysis and science mapping supply complementary instruments. Performance indicators identify productive authors, sources, and countries, whereas relational analyses expose structures that publication counts cannot reveal [48,49]. Co-occurrence networks resolve thematic communities; strategic diagrams differentiate motor, basic, niche, and emerging themes by reference to centrality and density; thematic-evolution procedures trace continuity and transformation across periods [50]; and citation-based methods reconstruct intellectual lineage. Contemporary guidance has formalised the design of such studies [51] and their articulation with systematic review [52], while comparative appraisals delineate the capacities of available software environments [53,54]. Open-data infrastructures have in parallel been used to compare vocabulary and inventory practice across cities directly [55].

Bibliometric work on urban greenspace and urban biodiversity is not itself novel, and the adjacent literature is substantial. Farkas et al. mapped thirty years of urban green-space research from approximately four thousand Web of Science records [56]. More directly related studies have mapped biodiversity in urban green space using 3806 Web of Science records [57] and urban tree-diversity research from 2000 to 2022 [58]; a journal-level synthesis has also reviewed two decades of Urban Forestry & Urban Greening [59], and a general bibliometric analysis of urban-forest research has recently been published [60]. Further bibliometric treatments address carbon sinks in urban public green spaces [61], the intersection of green space with health behaviours [62], green infrastructure and urban ecosystem services [63], and the disciplinary heterogeneity of green-infrastructure definitions themselves [64]. The present study therefore does not claim to be the first bibliometric mapping of urban biodiversity or urban forestry. It differs in four design respects: the retrieval targets the intersection of biodiversity terminology with designations of urban tree, forest, and green-space resources, so that the corpus covers biodiversity research on urban green spaces as well as on urban forests (Section 2.1); the corpus is drawn from the multi-publisher OpenAlex infrastructure and audited for retrieval integrity; the conceptual analysis is computed on author-generated title and abstract text rather than on algorithmically assigned classification labels; and conceptual, country-level collaboration, co-citation, and bibliographic-coupling structures are examined within one audited corpus. Whether these design choices produce materially different structures from prior corpora is tested in Section Document-Level Comparison with a Prior Corpus by a document-level comparison with a replica, within OpenAlex, of the search strategy of Zhao et al. [57]. The urban-forestry terms are what distinguish the present corpus: 80.1% of its documents absent from [57] entered through these terms, and the conceptual structures of the two corpora agree only moderately (NMI = 0.382), whereas the leading countries for 2006–2021 coincide.

The second of these design choices requires justification. OpenAlex has emerged as a credible open alternative to proprietary indexes, with reference coverage broadly comparable to the Web of Science and Scopus for recent publications shared across the three databases [65], substantially broader coverage of open-access journals [66], and, as a third-party database, greater overall metadata completeness than academic search engines in comparative testing [67]. It is nonetheless not a neutral instrument. Document-type taxonomies diverge across databases [68], paper-based subject classifications underwent extensive reassignment during the transition from Microsoft Academic Graph to OpenAlex [69], and a comparative appraisal concludes that metadata accuracy and completeness require continued scrutiny [70]. Section 2.3 sets out why the platform’s classification-derived vocabulary fields were rejected as the basis of conceptual mapping in favour of the corpus’s own text.

Accordingly, this study provides an integrated bibliometric cartography of biodiversity research on urban forests and green spaces retrieved from OpenAlex. It is designed as a science-mapping review: quantitative structures are used to organise the literature, and their implications for biodiversity research are then assessed critically (Section 4.7). It addresses six research questions (RQ). RQ1: How did retrieved scientific production evolve across the complete years 2006–2025 and the partial year 2026? RQ2: Which publishers, journals, authors, and countries structure the corpus? RQ3: How is international collaboration organised? RQ4: Which conceptual clusters and strategic themes characterise the literature? RQ5: How are those themes related across successive periods? RQ6: Which citation-based structures characterise the field’s co-cited core and bibliographic-coupling research fronts? A seventh, interpretive question follows from RQ4–RQ6. RQ7: What do these structures indicate about how biodiversity is studied in urban forests and green spaces—which organisms, measures, and theoretical frames dominate, and which are rare?

Beyond these descriptive questions, the study makes two methodological contributions relative to existing bibliometric mappings of this domain. First, it documents a silent failure mode of rate-limited multi-page OpenAlex extraction, in which failed pages are replaced by replicated successful pages without an error being raised, and specifies the integrity check that detects it. Second, it reports the stability of stochastic community partitions across 200 repeated runs rather than a single partition, making explicit where a reported solution competes with near-equivalent alternatives. Both practices bear on the reproducibility of any OpenAlex-based science map. Substantively, by computing the conceptual map on author-generated text rather than on platform classification labels, the study examines whether carbon, health, and nature-based-solution vocabularies form domains distinct from the ecosystem-service core, and how these domains relate to the co-cited canon and to current research fronts. The divergence between national publication volume and brokerage position (Section 3.4) is reported as an empirical finding obtained with standard network indicators, not as a methodological contribution.

sec.title: 2.1. Corpus Constitution
sec.p: The corpus was constructed by direct interrogation of the OpenAlex REST API. OpenAlex was selected in preference to a publisher platform because source-level indicators—outlet rankings, Bradford stratification, and publisher distribution—are interpretable only when computed over a multi-publisher document population.

The retrieval expression combined two term blocks under conjunction. The first enumerated designations of the urban forest resource: urban forest, urban forests, urban forestry, urban tree, urban trees, street tree, street trees, urban green space, urban green spaces, urban greening, urban woodland, and urban woodlands. The second enumerated designations of biological diversity: biodiversity, species richness, species diversity, plant diversity, tree diversity, and biological diversity. Both blocks were matched against titles and abstracts. OpenAlex search filters apply stemming and stop-word removal; inflectional variants were nevertheless enumerated explicitly so that the intended retrieval vocabulary remained transparent in the archived query [71]. The complete API call is reproduced in Appendix A. On 13 October 2026, the final intersected expression returned 3970 works.

The retrieval expression is deliberately narrow, and its boundaries condition every result that follows. It does not enumerate urban park, urban vegetation, green infrastructure, urban green, city tree, or peri-urban forest. Documents on urban parks or green infrastructure therefore enter the corpus only when they also carry one of the twelve enumerated resource terms. No recall or precision test against an external benchmark set was performed. No filter on paratext or retracted status was applied either, so editorial material, corrections, and retracted items typed as journal articles by the platform remain eligible for inclusion. The consequences of both choices are stated in Section 4.8.

Document types were restricted to journal articles and reviews. The corpus covers publications from 1 January 2006 to 17 August 2026, the date of the original retrieval; the extraction analysed here, performed on 13 October 2026 (Section 2.2), kept this upper bound, so the final publication year is incomplete. The exact form of the date filter is given in Appendix A. The lower bound of 1 January 2006 follows an empirical test made at the original retrieval: an otherwise identical query without a lower bound returned 4086 works, of which 129 (3.2%) predated 2006. Annual output before 2000 did not exceed five documents, and the acceleration visible in the retrieved series begins around 2002–2003. The 2006 bound is therefore a pragmatic analytical boundary rather than an emergence threshold.

The resource block includes “urban green space(s)” and “urban greening” as well as tree, forest, and woodland terms. These terms follow how the field itself is delimited: its leading journal, Urban Forestry & Urban Greening (Section 3.2), joins urban forestry and urban greening in its title, and urban forests, green infrastructure, and urban green space are treated in the literature as overlapping framings rather than separate objects [26,64]. The green-space terms nonetheless broaden the corpus well beyond urban forestry. Of the 3970 works reported by the API on 13 October 2026, 2174 (54.8%) were retrieved only through the green-space terms; in the final corpus, 2056 of 3747 documents (54.9%) are in this situation, and only 34.9% of those with an OpenAlex abstract mention trees, forests, woodland, woody vegetation, canopy, or shrubs in their title or abstract. The corpus therefore covers biodiversity research on urban green spaces as well as on urban forests, and its conceptual map is scope-dependent in this respect (Section 3.6).

sec.title: 2.2. Retrieval Integrity and Deduplication
sec.p: The analyses reported in this article rest on an extraction performed on 13 October 2026 with the date bounds of Section 2.1. The count reported by the API before extraction, 3970 works, served as the completeness target. Extraction returned 3980 rows, of which 10 were pagination duplicates; the 3970 distinct work identifiers match the reported count exactly. An earlier extraction of 17 August 2026, on which the first version of this study was based, had returned 3953 of 3957 reported works and a final corpus of 3767 documents; its raw files and scripts were not retained, so all results were recomputed on the extraction of 13 October 2026 with scripts that are provided as Supplementary File S1.

Extraction integrity was verified after every API call by comparing three quantities: returned rows, distinct work identifiers, and the count reported by the API. This verification is not a formality. During the original extraction, rate-limited multi-page requests were observed to fail silently under the client version then used: rather than raising an error, the client returned an object in which successfully retrieved pages had been replicated to fill the positions of failed pages, yielding a data frame of nominally correct size in which 200 unique works appeared eighteen times each. Any extraction in which distinct identifiers departed from the reported count by more than 0.5%, or in which rows were replicated beyond isolated pagination duplicates, was discarded and re-executed; cited-reference metadata were retrieved in batches of fifty with explicit inter-batch delays.

Records were then deduplicated on normalised titles. Sixty-one records (1.5% of 3970) carried a title shared with at least one other record, arising from repository deposits of published articles, aggregator indexing, capitalisation variants within a single journal, and duplicate identifiers in OpenAlex. Where a work appeared in multiple locations, the journal version was retained in preference to aggregator entries, records of unresolved source, and repository deposits; ties were resolved by citation count and then DOI availability. Records whose source resolved to a repository rather than to a serial were then excluded; inspection at the original retrieval had indicated that many such records were project deliverables or policy briefs rather than journal literature. Because title-based matching can in principle conflate distinct works with identical or near-identical titles, the absence of a DOI-first sensitivity check is acknowledged in Section 4.8.

Title deduplication removed 32 records, and the repository exclusion removed 191, leaving a final analytical corpus comprising 3747 documents. Source-level analyses are computed on the 3629 documents whose venue was resolved to a journal; the remaining 118, whose source was unresolved or resolved only to an aggregating index, are retained for all document-level analyses and excluded from source-level analyses alone. Table 1 records the complete audit trail of retrieval and processing, and Figure 1 summarises it as a flow diagram.

sec.title: 2.3. Why the Platform’s Classification Fields Were Not Used
sec.p: OpenAlex exposes several aboutness fields, of which concepts and keywords were examined for suitability as the basis of conceptual mapping. Neither is an author-declared lexicon, and both are unsuitable here for reasons documented by the provider [71].

The concepts scheme, inherited from the Microsoft Academic Graph and linked to Wikidata, was deprecated in 2024 in favour of topics; it is no longer maintained or extended, and, according to the provider, works were tagged by a machine-learning classifier and ancestors of every tagged concept were also attached, so that concept lists frequently include broad, low-scoring entries; the scheme was retired because its accuracy was uneven, particularly at deeper levels [71]. The keywords field is not text-derived in the sense required here either: keywords are drawn from curated keyword sets attached to the topics a work has been assigned, with at most five per work, each carrying a similarity score against the work’s title and abstract. Both fields are therefore products of classification against a fixed external vocabulary, and neither is independent of the other in practice, since both descend from machine classification of the same metadata.

Inspection of the corpus of the first submission is consistent with that architecture. Across the seventeen most frequent terms, the ratio of keyword frequency to concept frequency was approximately constant at 0.80 (range 0.68–0.93) and rank order was identical. Both fields carried ontology artefacts, including parenthetical sense qualifiers such as Vegetation (pathology), Diversity (politics), Tree (set theory), and Space (punctuation), together with disciplinary labels of no substantive content in this domain (Business, Archaeology, Mathematics, Computer science). Neither field is suitable as the sole basis for conceptual mapping in a domain of this kind.

Conceptual analysis was based on terms extracted from document text. Titles were available for all 3747 documents and abstracts for 3096 (82.6%) after the supplementation described below; titles and available abstracts were concatenated, hyphens converted to spaces to recover compounds split by orthographic variation, and bigrams extracted after removal of stop words, numerals, and tokens shorter than three characters. Inflectional variants were merged by rule-based normalisation carrying an explicit exception list, since naive suffix stripping corrupts invariant forms such as species and loss. Bigrams reproducing the retrieval expression were excluded from the conceptual map to reduce retrieval-induced dominance: biological diversity, plant diversity, species diversity, species richness, tree diversity, street tree, urban forest, urban forestry, urban greening, urban tree, urban woodland, green space, and urban green, the last two being the bigrams of the trigram urban green space, together with the inflectional variants enumerated in Section 2.1. This design choice also removes potentially discriminating variation among alternative query phrases and is therefore treated as a limitation rather than as a logically necessary exclusion. Generic phrases of scientific discourse without thematic content (for example, result show, important role, case study, significant difference, long term), place-name fragments (york city), and two extraction artefacts (a leading “Abstract” label and the abbreviation UGS) were also excluded; the complete stop-word, exception, and exclusion lists are given in the scripts of Supplementary File S1. A dedicated -ise/-ize orthographic harmonisation step was not applied; British and American spelling variants may therefore remain distinct in the term counts.

Abstract availability is strongly publisher-dependent. In the corpus, 872 of 3747 documents (23.3%) lack an OpenAlex abstract, and 843 of these (96.7%) are published by Elsevier (61.8% of its documents lack an abstract) or Springer (64.9%, and 14 of the 25 documents indexed under Springer Nature), which publish the three leading journals of the corpus (Section 3.2); no other publisher with more than 20 documents exceeds 5% (Table A1 and Table A2). Abstracts were therefore sought by DOI from the Crossref REST API and then from the Semantic Scholar API for the 861 documents lacking an abstract but having a DOI. Crossref returned 1 abstract and Semantic Scholar 220, raising abstract coverage from 76.7% to 82.6%. All conceptual analyses use these supplemented abstracts; the effect of unequal text availability on the lexical clusters is assessed in Section 3.6.

sec.title: 2.4. Analytical Procedures
sec.p: All indicators were computed directly from the OpenAlex data structures using purpose-written R routines rather than the standard Bibliometrix conversion pipeline. Direct computation made each analytical operation explicit; the scripts, the audit values, and the derived tables are provided as Supplementary File S1, so that every value reported here can be regenerated from the API. The derived values were not cross-validated against an independent implementation; this limitation is stated in Section 4.8.

Citation aggregates are reported with the median alongside the mean, the distribution being strongly right-skewed, together with corpus-level h- and g-indices; the latter increase monotonically with corpus size and are descriptive properties of this document set rather than cross-study comparators. Citation counts are those recorded by OpenAlex on 13 October 2026. Country-level indicators are reported on two bases: corresponding-author attribution, available for 2485 works (66.3%), and full-affiliation attribution, available for 3224 works (86.0%). Both are reported because the two answer different questions, and because the corresponding-author field is a documented weak point of bibliographic metadata in general. The available assessment of that field [75] examines the Web of Science and Scopus rather than OpenAlex, and is cited here as an indication that the field warrants caution in any database, not as evidence about OpenAlex specifically.

The country collaboration network was built from the co-occurrence of affiliation countries within documents; edges below weight three were removed and isolates discarded. Betweenness was computed using inverse tie strength as distance, alongside PageRank and degree. Lexical co-occurrence was computed over a fixed vocabulary of the 110 most frequent bigrams, normalised by the Callon equivalence index, and pruned to the eight strongest ties per term. These network-construction choices are treated as analytical parameters rather than universal thresholds, and their untested sensitivity is reported in Section 4.8.

Community structure was assessed by Louvain modularity optimisation [76]. Louvain is stochastic, so a partition obtained from a single execution is only one admissible solution. Each reported partition was therefore recomputed 200 times from a fixed master seed (20261013), so that the run sequence is reproducible; the distribution of cluster counts and modularity values was recorded, the modularity-maximising solution was retained for presentation, and the best solution with the most frequent alternative cluster count was compared with it. For the lexical network, the six-cluster solution at Q = 0.442 occurred in 41.5% of runs and a seven-cluster solution in 58.0%; the two differ only in whether three carbon and allometry terms form a separate cluster (normalised mutual information, NMI, 0.795; Section 3.6). For the co-citation network, six communities at Q = 0.507 occurred in 49.0% of runs and five in 48.5%; the five-community solution merges a two-reference community into a neighbouring one (NMI 0.987; Section 3.10). These near-competing solutions are reported explicitly and should not be read as unique structures. Louvain rather than Leiden was used for continuity with much of the bibliometric literature, notwithstanding that Louvain can return internally disconnected communities [77]; the absence of a Leiden sensitivity analysis is revisited in Section 4.8.

Intellectual structure was examined through the cited-reference field, which yields 173,116 citation links to 92,268 distinct cited works. Software citations were excluded, since they index methodological practice rather than intellectual lineage; the prominence of software among cited references is itself an established object of scientometric study [78]. The complete cited set was screened with an over-inclusive pattern match on title, type, and source, which flagged 597 candidate works (2083 links, 1.20% of all links); all flagged items were excluded. In the first version of this study, only the 500 most cited references had been inspected manually; excluding all flagged items rather than only those in that band leaves the bibliographic-coupling structure essentially unchanged (17 principal fronts in both versions; NMI = 0.871; Table A3). Bibliographic coupling was computed by sparse matrix multiplication and normalised by the Salton cosine, which is necessary to prevent reference-rich reviews from dominating through volume. Co-citation was computed over the 200 most frequently cited references and co-citation strengths were likewise Salton-normalised, with an edge threshold of eight co-citations. Before selection, cited records sharing a normalised title and a publication year differing by at most one were merged (three pairs), and three cited identifiers without retrievable metadata in OpenAlex (346 links) were excluded because neither their identity nor their nature could be verified.

sec.title: 2.5. Rules of Interpretation
sec.p: The final publication year is incomplete; no inference about growth, deceleration, or contraction in 2026 is made from the partial-year count. The incompleteness of 2026 also affects the thematic analysis: its 484 documents constitute 22.0% of the 2202 documents in the 2022–2026 period, so the themes reported for that period rest partly on an incomplete year, and their weights are not directly comparable with those of the two earlier periods. No recomputation excluding 2026 was performed. Source-level indicators are computed on 3629 documents and country-level indicators on 2485 or 3224 documents, as stated. Language metadata are missing for 4.8% of documents and imperfectly accurate where present; no language filter was applied, and English-language works constitute 92.6% of the corpus. Networks are interpreted as relational structures rather than causal models, and network indicators as properties of the graph rather than proxies for scientific quality. Where the text describes temporal linkage between themes, the claim refers to vocabulary overlap or citation adjacency and does not imply causal or intellectual descent.

A notational convention applies throughout the Results. Individual records—both documents of the analysed corpus and works appearing in its cited-reference data—are designated in tables by first-author surname and the publication year recorded in OpenAlex. Such labels identify records within the data and do not constitute bibliographic citations; the OpenAlex year occasionally precedes the issue year of the corresponding publication by one year, and where a labelled record is also discussed substantively in the argument, the full reference appears in the reference list under its issue year.

sec.title: 2.6. Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
sec.p: During the preparation of this manuscript, the authors used Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, San Francisco, CA, USA) to assist with drafting, language editing, and revision of the text; with verification of the bibliographic references against Crossref records; and with checking the internal consistency of values reported across the text, tables, and figures. All AI-assisted content was reviewed, edited, and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content of this publication. During the revision, the same tool was also used to draft the R scripts for the extraction and all analyses; the authors executed and checked these scripts and take full responsibility for their outputs.

sec.title: 3.1. General Characteristics and Temporal Growth
sec.p: The analytical corpus comprises 3747 documents published from 2006 through 17 August 2026, distributed across 1316 journals and 407 publishers. The corpus involves 12,079 distinct authors, with a mean of 4.41 authors per document. English-language works account for 92.6% of the corpus, and language metadata are absent for 180 works (4.8%). No language filter was applied. Table 2 summarises the principal characteristics of the corpus.

Retrieved annual output increased from 42 documents in 2006 to 692 in 2025, corresponding to a compound annual growth rate of 15.89% across the complete-year interval 2006–2025. The 484 documents recorded for 2026 are a partial-year count, because the publication window closes on 17 August 2026, and are not extrapolated. Annual output first exceeded one hundred documents in 2014 (105), fell to 90 in 2015, and then rose each year through 2025. A 2015–2025 compound rate of 22.63% is strongly influenced by the 2015 local minimum; using 2014 as the baseline yields 18.70%. The complete annual series is shown in Figure 2, and the growth estimates should be interpreted as properties of the retrieved corpus rather than as database-normalised measures of field growth.

These growth figures are absolute and are not normalised against changes in OpenAlex coverage or world scientific output over the same period. An unknown portion of the observed increase may therefore reflect database expansion and broader growth in scholarly publishing rather than growth specific to this research domain; this limitation is developed in Section 4.8.

sec.title: 3.2. Publishers, Sources, and Bradford Stratification
sec.p: Publication is dispersed across a broad population of outlets. Elsevier is the largest publisher with 880 documents, 23.5% of the corpus, ahead of Springer (439), MDPI (389), Wiley (212), Taylor & Francis (91), and Frontiers (84); 245 of the 407 publishers contribute a single document each. Publisher and journal shares alike are reported against the full corpus of 3747 documents rather than against the reduced set of 3629 with a resolved journal source, so that every percentage in this section rests on one unambiguous denominator; computed on the reduced set, each value would be higher by a factor of 1.033.

At journal level (Table 3), Urban Forestry & Urban Greening is the leading outlet with 341 documents, or 9.10% of the corpus, followed by Urban Ecosystems (235; 6.27%) and Landscape and Urban Planning (143; 3.82%). No journal exceeds one document in ten on either denominator. The distribution shows a Bradford-like long tail: 897 journals (68.2% of the 1316 contributing journals) carry exactly one document, and the set of journals jointly accounting for approximately one third of the journal-resolved output (3629 documents) comprises seventeen titles. This descriptive concentration is not presented as a formal goodness-of-fit test of Bradford’s law.

The composition of this ranking is itself informative. Alongside specialist urban-forestry and landscape-planning outlets, it includes multidisciplinary megajournals (PLoS ONE, Scientific Reports), open-access environmental serials (Sustainability, Forests, Land), a remote-sensing title, and a Chinese-language landscape architecture journal. The literature is therefore not confined to a disciplinary core but distributed across specialist, generalist, and methodological venues.

sec.title: 3.3. Authors
sec.p: Authorship is highly dispersed: 12,079 distinct authors contribute 3747 documents, and no individual exceeds 25 documents, or 0.7% of corpus output. Ingo Kowarik is the most productive contributor (25), followed by C. Y. Jim (22) and Stephen J. Livesley (18). A further group contributes twelve to fourteen documents each, comprising Cecil C. Konijnendijk, Nicholas S. G. Williams, Meghan L. Avolio, Caragh G. Threlfall, Dagmar Haase, Marco Moretti, Francisco J. Escobedo, Mir Muhammad Nizamani, and Karl L. Evans. These counts rest on OpenAlex author identifiers and are therefore subject to the disambiguation error characteristic of automated author resolution, which can both split a single author across identifiers and merge distinct authors under one; no manual verification of the ranked authors was undertaken. Subject to that qualification, the absence of any dominant signature is consistent with a field organised around distributed rather than concentrated authorship.

sec.title: 3.4. Geography and Country-Level International Collaboration
sec.p: Author affiliations span 124 countries. Country attribution is reported on two bases, since the two answer different questions and have different coverage. On corresponding-author attribution, available for 2485 documents (66.3%), China ranks first with 421 documents, ahead of the USA (271), Germany (160), Australia (136), Italy (131), and the United Kingdom (128). On full-affiliation attribution, available for 3224 documents (86.0%), China again ranks first (502), followed by the USA (423), Germany (245), Brazil (235), the United Kingdom (215), and Australia (190). Both bases place China ahead of the USA, by a factor of 1.55 on the corresponding-author basis. Of the 124 countries, 54 are retained in the collaboration network analysed below, the remainder falling below the weight-three edge threshold or becoming isolates once it is applied; the fifteen countries of Table 4 are the union of the ten leading countries on each attribution basis and the ten highest in betweenness, so the table is not a strict production ranking.
International co-authorship—documents whose authors are affiliated to more than one country—stands at 25.43% of the 3224 documents with at least one affiliation country.

Production volume and network position diverge markedly. China leads output on both attribution bases yet ranks third in betweenness centrality (256.0), at about half the values recorded by Germany (507.0) and the USA (500.0), and fourth in PageRank, behind the USA, Germany, and the United Kingdom. Germany and the USA are separated by less than 2% in betweenness and are best read as jointly occupying the dominant brokerage position rather than as ranked. Italy presents the converse profile: a degree of 27 and a PageRank of 0.0377, against a betweenness of zero, indicating a country well connected within an already dense neighbourhood and not positioned on shortest paths between otherwise separated groups; India and Canada show the same pattern. Malaysia shows the opposite configuration at small scale, with only four ties but a betweenness of 100.0, because it lies on the only short paths to a few peripheral countries. Volume of production and structural integration into the international collaboration system are therefore distinct properties, and should not be inferred from one another.

Louvain community detection on the collaboration network returns four partitions at a modularity of 0.162. As this falls well below the conventional interpretive threshold of 0.30, no community interpretation is offered. Two qualifications attach to this negative result. The 0.30 threshold is a rule of thumb rather than a test statistic, and its meaning depends on the size and density of the graph; the value is computed after removal of ties of weight below three, a filter that densifies the retained core and therefore depresses modularity. No comparison against degree-preserving randomisations and no threshold-sensitivity analysis was performed, so the finding is reported as an absence of detectable partition structure under the stated construction rather than as evidence that the field is unpartitioned.

sec.title: 3.5. Citation Impact
sec.p: The 3747 documents had received 89,941 citations at the extraction date, a mean of 24.00 per document but a median of only 5. The ratio of mean to median (4.80) indicates a strongly right-skewed distribution in which a small number of publications account for a disproportionate share of citations. The corpus h-index is 131 and the g-index 213; both increase monotonically with corpus size and are reported as descriptive properties of this document set rather than as cross-study comparators.

sec.title: 3.6. Conceptual Structure
sec.p: Conceptual analysis was performed on bigrams extracted from document titles and abstracts (Section 2.3). All 3747 documents contributed title text, and 3096 also contributed abstract text. The vocabulary was fixed at the 110 most frequent bigrams, each occurring in at least 61 documents; a fixed size was preferred to a frequency threshold because a threshold of thirty documents would retain 426 terms, a network too dense to read, and because a fixed vocabulary keeps the sensitivity variants of Table A4 directly comparable. Co-occurrence was normalised by the Callon equivalence index and the network pruned to the eight strongest ties per term. Applying the stability procedure of Section 2.4, Louvain community detection resolved six clusters at Q = 0.442 in 41.5% of 200 runs. A seven-cluster partition occurred in 58.0% of runs at marginally lower modularity (best Q = 0.441); it differs from the six-cluster solution only in that carbon sequestration, carbon storage, and breast height form a cluster of their own instead of belonging to the tree and plant species cluster (NMI = 0.795). The six-cluster solution is reported because it maximises modularity, but it should be read as one of two closely competing structures rather than as a unique partition. Table 5 reports the six-cluster solution and Figure 3 the corresponding network.

The interpretive labels in the first column were assigned by the authors after reading the full member-term lists; labelling was not independently coded, and no inter-rater agreement statistic is available. The labels are descriptive conveniences and carry no independent analytical weight.

The sensitivity of this partition to text availability and to the scope of the query was assessed with the vocabulary held fixed and the same 200-run procedure (Table A4). Relative to the partition of Table 5, the NMI is 0.872 for the abstract-complete subcorpus (3096 documents) and 0.708 when only OpenAlex abstracts are used; in both variants the six domains recur, the only systematic difference being that the carbon terms form a separate cluster, as in the competing seven-cluster solution. When the 2056 documents retrieved only through the green-space terms are removed (1691 documents remain), the NMI falls to 0.404. The green-infrastructure and planning, tree and plant species, and urban heat domains recur, but the ecosystem-service terms group with climate, carbon, and forest-management terms; landscape and habitat terms form a separate cluster that absorbs much of the park and bird vocabulary, canopy terms join remote sensing and tree planting, and four functional-trait terms separate. The domains in Table 5 are therefore robust to text availability but not to query scope: the green-space literature shapes the ecosystem-service, landscape, and park vocabularies of the map (Section 4.8).

Two features of the partition concern domains that the literature often treats separately. Health vocabulary (human health, public health, mental health, air pollution) does not form a cluster of its own but belongs to the climate-change and green-infrastructure cluster, together with urban planning, urban development, and green roofs. Carbon vocabulary attaches to the tree and plant species cluster or, in the competing seven-cluster solution, forms a cluster of its own. Whether an equivalent analysis based on the platform’s topic assignments would recover the same domains was not tested and is identified as a robustness priority in Section 5.

The position of the carbon vocabulary merits comment. Carbon sequestration and carbon storage, together with breast height, the stem-diameter measure on which allometric biomass estimates rest, belong to the tree and plant species cluster rather than to the ecosystem-service cluster, which contains most of the remaining service vocabulary. Under the competing seven-cluster partition, these three terms form a cluster of their own; whichever of the two admissible partitions is adopted, the carbon terms do not join the service vocabulary.

sec.title: 3.7. Strategic Thematic Map
sec.p: Clusters were positioned by centrality (external association, normalised by the number of possible external pairs) and density (internal association, normalised by the number of possible internal pairs). All six clusters are retained. Pair-count normalisation reduces the mechanical effect of cluster size, but it does not eliminate the greater instability expected for very small clusters; the three-term canopy and four-term urban-heat clusters should therefore be interpreted more cautiously than larger clusters. Table 6 gives the coordinates and Figure 4 the corresponding diagram.

The observed quadrant distribution varies with cluster size. The only cluster located in the motor quadrant, urban heat and air quality, is among the smallest in the corpus, comprising four terms and 3.9% of term volume, and combines the highest centrality (0.284) with the highest density (27.27). Because it contains few terms, its density is sensitive to a small number of links and should be read descriptively rather than as evidence of a statistically distinct class. The two niche clusters differ greatly in size: canopy assessment (three terms) is dense (7.85) but peripheral, whereas tree and plant species (23 terms) lies only just above the density median (0.787 against 0.758).

Conversely, the two largest clusters occupy the basic/transversal quadrant. Urban biodiversity, ecosystem services and landscape comprises forty terms and 41.3% of term volume yet records the lowest internal density in the corpus (0.308); climate change, green infrastructure, planning and health (26 terms, 24.4% of volume) records the second-highest centrality (0.137) with below-median density. The parks and faunal communities cluster lies in the low-centrality/low-density quadrant conventionally labelled emerging or declining. Because that quadrant does not distinguish emergence from decline, temporal evidence is required before either interpretation is adopted. The low density of the largest vocabularies is consistent with their use across heterogeneous research contexts, but it does not by itself establish a specific methodological programme [27].

Two positions warrant separate comment. The tree and plant species cluster is classed as niche only by a narrow density margin and moves to the low-centrality/low-density quadrant under mean centring; because its constituent vocabulary has comparatively early median publication years (Section 3.9), a mature descriptive core is one plausible interpretation, but the strategic diagram alone cannot distinguish maturity, decline, or fragmentation. The health vocabulary shares the basic/transversal position of the climate and green-infrastructure cluster to which it belongs, a position compatible with health being framed as one outcome of green-infrastructure planning rather than as a separate theme. Quadrant labels are therefore treated as descriptive heuristics rather than temporal diagnoses.

sec.title: 3.8. Thematic Evolution
sec.p: Thematic structure was recomputed independently for three periods: 2006–2016 (700 documents), 2017–2021 (845), and 2022–2026 (2202), each with the 110 most frequent bigrams of the period and the 200-run procedure. The periods are very unequal in size, which reflects corpus growth but limits direct comparison of cluster counts and raw weights; the final period also includes an incomplete year contributing 22.0% of its documents (Section 2.5). The three counts sum to 3747, so every document is assigned. Continuity between periods is measured by the inclusion index, the proportion of shared terms relative to the smaller of the two clusters, and links of at least 0.20 are reported. Table 7 reports the themes identified in each period. These period-specific results should be interpreted as a descriptive partition of the retrieved corpus, not as direct evidence that a topic originated or disappeared in a particular interval.

Three persistent themes and several cross-period vocabulary links are observed. The ecosystem-service theme is present in all three periods: the 2006–2016 cluster labelled urban area, which contains ecosystem services as its second term, links to the ecosystem-service theme of 2017–2021 (inclusion 0.433), which links to its successor at 0.406. Plant species and tree species are also present as themes in all three periods, with plant species linking at 0.500 and then 0.875, and tree species at 0.333 and 0.375. Against this stable background, the health, heat, and remote-sensing vocabularies change position between periods.

Health vocabulary forms a distinct theme only in 2017–2021 (human health, weight 392, fourth of six), whose backward link is with biodiversity conservation in 2006–2016 (inclusion 0.250). In 2022–2026, it no longer forms a separate theme: its strongest forward link is with the climate-change theme (0.333), which contains human health, public health, mental health, and air pollution alongside green-infrastructure and planning terms, as in the global partition (Table 5). Because inclusion indices of 0.25–0.33 mean that at most a third of the terms of the smaller cluster are shared, the result supports relative lexical proximity among the compared themes, not derivation or historical origin, and the final period contains an incomplete year.

Urban-heat vocabulary shows the strongest continuity of any small theme. In 2006–2016, heat island, urban heat, air quality, and green roofs belong to the cluster labelled urban parks; this cluster links to urban development in 2017–2021 (inclusion 0.714), which in turn links to the heat-island theme of 2022–2026 (0.625). These values must be read against the small size of the clusters concerned: inclusion indices of this magnitude can arise from a handful of shared terms, and no null expectation under random assignment was computed, so the result is reported as vocabulary containment rather than as demonstrated thematic derivation.

Three further elements of Table 7 are reported descriptively. Remote sensing forms a theme only in 2022–2026 (334), linked to the ecosystem-service (0.400) and tree-species (0.200) themes of 2017–2021; canopy cover (217) links to tree species (0.500); and the urban-park theme of 2022–2026 (967), which also contains the bird vocabulary, links to urban landscape (0.231), plant species (0.214), and tree species (0.200), so it may reflect vocabulary previously distributed across these themes rather than a wholly new topic. In the final period, carbon sequestration and carbon storage belong to the tree-species theme. The inclusion index alone cannot distinguish relabelling, fragmentation, consolidation, emergence, or disappearance, so no such temporal mechanism is inferred.

Figure 5 renders the reported cross-period vocabulary links as an alluvial diagram, with band width proportional to the inclusion index and vertical position carrying no meaning. The ecosystem-service theme remains linked across all three periods while sharing vocabulary with adjacent themes; the health theme of 2017–2021 flows into the climate-change theme of 2022–2026; and the heat vocabulary forms a chain from the urban-park cluster of 2006–2016 to the heat-island theme of 2022–2026.
All three period-specific analyses use the preprocessing and exclusion lists of the global analysis (Section 2.3), so that differences between periods do not arise from differences in preprocessing.

sec.title: 3.9. Trend Topics
sec.p: Term-level temporal positions are consistent with the same pattern. Among the terms displayed in Figure 6 (the three most frequent in each lexical cluster), the earliest median years attach to tree species, species composition, and community composition (2022). Ecosystem services, urban area, plant species, urban parks, and bird species have a median of 2023; climate change, green infrastructure, urban environment, heat island, canopy cover, and tree canopy have a median of 2024; tree cover has a median of 2024.5; and urban planning, urban heat, and air quality have a median of 2025. Across the full vocabulary, the latest medians (2025) also attach to sustainable urban development, carbon sequestration, carbon storage, biodiversity loss, public health, climate adaptation, and climate resilience, whereas forest fragment (2020) and protected area (2021.5) have the earliest. The correspondence with the thematic-evolution analysis of Section 3.8 is partial rather than exact: the climate, planning, and heat vocabularies are recent in both, but canopy cover and remote sensing, which form themes only in 2022–2026, have medians of 2024. The two statistics agree on the recency of climate-, planning-, and health-oriented vocabulary taken as a whole, and not term by term.

The interpretive value of this statistic is limited by the temporal shape of the corpus. Because 58.8% of documents fall in 2022–2026, term medians are compressed toward the recent end of a twenty-one-year span, and ordering within that window is sensitive to small differences in document counts. Trend-topic medians therefore provide a descriptive temporal summary that is partly dependent on corpus growth and should not be treated as independent evidence of emergence.

sec.title: 3.10. Intellectual Structure: Co-Cited Core
sec.p: The cited-reference field yields 173,116 citation links to 92,268 distinct cited works, a mean of 46.2 references per document. Candidate software works (597 works; 2083 links) were excluded, together with three cited identifiers without retrievable metadata (346 links), and three pairs of duplicate records of the same cited work were merged (Section 2.4).

Co-citation was computed over the 200 most cited references—approximately 0.2% of distinct cited works—to keep the network interpretable. The resulting communities therefore characterise the most heavily co-cited core rather than the citation base as a whole. At an edge threshold of eight, the network comprises 196 connected nodes and 1414 edges, with a density of 7.40% over connected nodes (7.11% over all 200 retained references, including four isolates). Applying the stability procedure, Louvain resolved six communities at Q = 0.507 in 49.0% of 200 runs; a five-community solution occurred in 48.5% of runs at marginally lower modularity and differs only in merging the two-reference domestic-garden community (C6) into the ecosystem-service community (C2) (NMI = 0.987). The six-community solution is thus a frequently recovered, modularity-maximising representation rather than a unique partition. No sensitivity analysis over the top-200 selection or the edge threshold of eight was performed. Table 8 reports the six-community solution and Figure 7 the corresponding network.

Three features of this partition merit emphasis. First, the field’s most co-cited works are drawn predominantly from general ecology and conservation journals—Biological Conservation, Science, Ecology Letters, BioScience, Proceedings of the Royal Society B, Trends in Ecology & Evolution, PNAS—rather than from specialist urban-forestry outlets. Second, the largest community (C1, 87 references) combines the urbanisation-and-biodiversity canon (McKinney; Grimm et al.; Aronson et al.; Beninde et al.) with the founding statements of urban ecology as a discipline (Niemelä; McDonnell and Pickett) and with MacArthur and Wilson’s island-biogeographic framework, which OpenAlex indexes under two records. The diversity-measurement canon lies elsewhere: Shannon, Simpson, and Magurran’s Measuring Biological Diversity (recorded in OpenAlex under another first author and the year 2005) fall within C4, the urban-forest and urban-tree diversity community, so the measurement literature is associated with tree-inventory studies rather than forming a centre of its own (Table 8). Third, the health community (C3) includes Fuller et al. [38], which reported positive associations between psychological well-being and species richness, alongside broader greenspace–health and perception works. It should therefore be read as a co-cited health-and-well-being canon rather than as evidence that biodiversity, instead of vegetation quantity, is generally the operative exposure; a later street-tree study, for example, found fewer antidepressant prescriptions with higher street-tree density near the home—marginally significant after adjustment for confounders and significant among residents of low socio-economic status—but no association with street-tree species richness [41].

sec.title: 3.11. Research Fronts: Bibliographic Coupling
sec.p: Bibliographic coupling links documents that share references and is commonly used to approximate research fronts. Coupling strengths were normalised by the Salton cosine to reduce domination by reference-rich documents. At a threshold of 0.08, the retained network comprises 2150 documents and 10,221 edges, resolving 86 fronts at Q = 0.720; seventeen fronts contain at least fifteen documents. Because the threshold retains only 57.4% of the full corpus, these fronts characterise the connected, reference-similar subnetwork rather than all 3747 documents. No threshold-sensitivity analysis was performed. Table 9 reports the seventeen fronts with at least fifteen documents, which together account for 1967 of the 2150 documents in the retained coupling network.

Median publication years differentiate established from emerging fronts, subject to the compression caveat of Section 3.9, which applies to these medians as it does to the term-level ones. The ground-beetle and arthropod front centres on 2018; the pollinator front on 2024 and the tree-microhabitat and deadwood front on 2025. The acoustic-index and deadwood fronts are the two smallest, holding 22 and 15 documents respectively, and are also recent (2023 and 2025), whereas the urban-woodland-edge front (26 documents) has a median of 2022.5, close to that of the corpus as a whole, and is small rather than new. These fronts represent candidate specialisations rather than consolidated programmes.

sec.title: 3.12. Correspondence Across the Three Structural Analyses
sec.p: The lexical, co-citation, and coupling analyses optimise unrelated criteria: shared vocabulary, shared third-party citations, and shared reference lists, respectively. Table 10 records the correspondence between them.

The correspondence was assessed against a reference set fixed before comparison, the six lexical clusters of Table 5, onto which co-citation communities and coupling fronts were matched under explicit rules: “yes”, a community or front whose principal members treat the domain’s subject as their main subject; “partial”, the domain’s subject forms an identifiable subset of a broader community or front; “no”, neither condition holds. The lexical column is therefore definitional. The 12 citation-side entries were coded independently, in a randomised order and from the same reference sheet of communities and fronts, by two authors working separately. Raw agreement was 10 of 12 (83.3%); Cohen’s κ was 0.44 (95% bootstrap confidence interval 0.00–1.00) and the linearly weighted κ 0.45 (0.00–1.00), indicating moderate agreement. Both disagreements concerned the parks and faunal communities domain: its coupling match was coded “yes” by one coder and “partial” by the other, and its co-citation match “partial” and “no”. Raw agreement is high, but κ is only moderate because nearly all entries fall in the “partial” category, a known property of κ under unbalanced category prevalence; with 12 entries, the bootstrap interval is uninformative. Where the codings disagreed, the more conservative code was retained. The pollinator co-citation community (C5) and six coupling fronts (F7, ground beetles and arthropods; F8, pollinators and wild bees; F14, lawns and meadows; F15, woodland edges and plant traits; F16, acoustic indices; F17, tree-related microhabitats) have no lexical counterpart in the reconciled codes, and are reported as citation structures without a lexical counterpart rather than added as domains. Accordingly, Table 10 is a structured qualitative crosswalk, not a quantitative test of agreement.

Against the six lexical domains, fixed before comparison, and using reconciled codes from two independent codings (Cohen’s κ = 0.44), no domain has a full match in both the co-citation and the coupling structures. The co-citation structure fully matches no domain and partially matches five; the coupling structure fully matches one domain and partially matches the other five. The partial category therefore carries almost all correspondences: each lexical domain is spread over several communities and fronts, so the citation structures are not aligned one-to-one with the vocabulary. Urban heat and air quality is the only domain with a full match, the coupling front on green infrastructure and urban cooling (F2), and parks and faunal communities is the only domain without a co-citation counterpart. These patterns are compatible with different relationships between current vocabulary, shared references, and the co-cited canon, but they do not constitute independent tests of those interpretations.

The co-citation communities are broader than the lexical domains. Four of the five domains with a co-citation counterpart are matched partially by three to five of the six communities, and the ecosystem-service community (C2) is matched to all five, the urbanisation-and-biodiversity community (C1) to four. Current domains therefore draw on a shared canon rather than on domain-specific canons, and the co-cited core is coarser than the working vocabulary.

sec.title: 4.1. A Field of Dispersed Organisation
sec.p: The literature is dispersed on every axis measured: no journal exceeds one document in ten, no author exceeds 0.7% of output, just over two thirds of contributing journals carry exactly one document, and the first Bradford zone, computed on the 3629 documents with a resolved journal source, comprises seventeen titles.

This bears on the recurrent question of whether urban forests, ecosystem services, green infrastructure, and nature-based solutions form a single analytical nexus or a set of partly overlapping framings [26], a question sharpened by the divergent definitions of green infrastructure across planning, ecology, and stormwater literatures [64]. Under the present network constructions, vocabulary, co-citation, and bibliographic coupling each yield a partitioned rather than unitary structure. However, the exact number and composition of partitions depend on the selected algorithm and thresholds, and the cross-structure correspondence in Table 10 is qualitative and subject to moderate inter-coder agreement (Cohen’s κ = 0.44). The evidence therefore supports a cautious description of partially connected programmes within this retrieved corpus, not a threshold-invariant taxonomy of the field.

sec.title: 4.2. Production and Integration Are Distinct National Properties
sec.p: China leads output on both attribution bases yet ranks third in betweenness centrality, at about half the values recorded by Germany and the USA; Italy presents the converse, with a high degree but zero betweenness. This divergence is obtained with standard centrality indicators; it is reported as a property of the present collaboration network rather than as a methodological novelty. Volume of production and structural integration into the international collaboration system are therefore distinct properties that cannot be inferred from one another. The distinction requires a network spanning the full country set to become visible, since it is a property of position among many countries rather than of any pair; no comparison against a restricted country set was computed here. Restricted to 2006–2021, the USA leads China in publication count both in the present corpus and in a replica of a prior search strategy (Section Document-Level Comparison with a Prior Corpus), so China’s lead over the full period reflects the publications of 2022–2026.

No community structure was detected in the collaboration network (modularity 0.162). The qualifications on this negative result are set out in Section 3.4 and should be read with it: the absence of a detected partition under the stated construction is not by itself evidence of an integrated system.

The presence of Brazil (235 documents on full-affiliation attribution) and India (176) among the leading contributors is worth noting alongside the geography of projected urban expansion, which concentrates in regions of high conservation value in Asia, Africa, and South America [1,4]. Whether research capacity is developing where the pressure is greatest is a question this corpus can begin to address but does not answer, since the analysis reports participation counts rather than per-capita or pressure-weighted measures.

sec.title: 4.3. Carbon Vocabulary Sits Apart from the Service Vocabulary
sec.p: The two closely competing lexical partitions differ only in the placement of the carbon terms—attached to the tree and plant species cluster or forming a small cluster of their own—and neither places them within the ecosystem-service cluster. One possible reading is that the retained vocabulary reflects measurement practice, because urban carbon quantities are often derived from species-level inventory and allometry [22]; the attachment of breast height, the inventory diameter measure, to the carbon terms is consistent with that reading. The co-occurrence structure alone cannot distinguish this explanation from other reasons for lexical separation, so the result is treated as a pattern in the mapped vocabulary rather than as evidence of a distinct scientific programme.

The strategic diagram adds a descriptive view of this pattern. The only motor cluster, urban heat and air quality, is a compact vocabulary accounting for 3.9% of term volume that combines the highest centrality with the highest density. The two largest clusters, accounting jointly for 65.7% of term volume, lie in the basic/transversal quadrant at the lowest internal densities in the corpus. This configuration is consistent with broad vocabularies being used across heterogeneous contexts and with a compact climate-oriented vocabulary being more internally cohesive, but the small number of clusters and the sensitivity of density for three- and four-term groups preclude stronger inference.

sec.title: 4.4. Health Vocabulary Is Embedded in Climate and Green-Infrastructure Framings
sec.p: Health vocabulary forms a distinct theme only in the 2017–2021 partition. In the global partition and in 2022–2026 it belongs to the cluster that also contains climate change, green infrastructure, urban planning, and green roofs, and the strongest forward link of the 2017–2021 health theme is with that climate-change theme (inclusion 0.333). The strength of this evidence should not be overstated: the analysis establishes relative lexical proximity among themes, not descent or historical origin, and the final period contains an incomplete year. A 2022–2025 sensitivity analysis is therefore needed before treating this merger as temporally robust.

Two further observations bear on this pattern without being diagnostic of it. The health vocabulary shares the basic/transversal position of its cluster, while the co-citation community on biodiversity perception and well-being (C3) includes work examining relationships between biodiversity or vegetation attributes and psychological or human-health outcomes [38,39,40,41]. Together these results show that health-related vocabulary and a health-relevant co-cited canon are present in the corpus, and that in current titles and abstracts health is framed together with climate adaptation and green-infrastructure planning. They do not establish a mechanism by which a health literature developed from conservation research.

sec.title: 4.5. The Co-Cited Core Draws Heavily on General Ecology and Conservation
sec.p: The most heavily co-cited works in the retained top-200 network are drawn predominantly from general ecology and conservation journals rather than from specialist urban-forestry outlets [6,7,8,9,10,12,16]. The specialist literature is prominent among publication venues, whereas the co-cited core draws heavily on broader ecological literature. Because co-citation was computed only over the 200 most cited references, this statement characterises the selected core and should not be generalised to the complete citation base.

Two structural features are noteworthy. Island biogeography lies within the largest community of the top-200 co-citation network, alongside the urbanisation and urban-ecology canon, showing that this framework remains part of the corpus’s heavily co-cited core. Diversity-measurement references such as Shannon, Simpson, and Magurran lie within the urban-forest and urban-tree diversity community rather than forming a centre of their own, a pattern compatible with a methodological toolkit associated above all with tree-inventory studies. Bibliographic coupling, which reflects shared reference lists among documents, separates fronts with different median publication years; because the coupling network retains only 57.4% of the corpus, these fronts are best treated as structures of the retained subnetwork rather than a complete map of current research.

sec.title: 4.6. Relation to Prior Bibliometric Treatments
sec.p: Several bibliometric treatments provide close points of comparison. Farkas et al. mapped approximately four thousand Web of Science records on urban green space [56]. Zhao et al. analysed 3806 Web of Science records specifically at the intersection of urban green space and biodiversity [57], while Xie et al. mapped urban tree-diversity research from 2000 to 2022 [58]. Guo and Chen reviewed two decades of Urban Forestry & Urban Greening and documented shifts toward biodiversity, ecosystem services, public health, and social-ecological integration [59]. The present study overlaps with all of these literatures but uses a different retrieval intersection, a different bibliographic infrastructure, author-text-derived conceptual mapping, and a joint analysis of collaboration, co-citation, and bibliographic coupling. Without document-level overlap or replication on another database, observed differences among studies cannot be attributed uniquely to substantive field structure rather than to database, query, period, or analytical choices.

The remaining adjacent reviews address narrower intersections that correspond to bounded components of the present mapping. The bibliometric review of carbon sinks in urban public green spaces [61] corresponds to the carbon vocabulary and a 130-document coupling front on urban-forest carbon storage; the treatment of urban green space and health behaviours [62] corresponds to health-related vocabulary and fronts; and the synthesis of green infrastructure and urban ecosystem services [63] overlaps with the two largest lexical clusters and co-citation community C2. These correspondences show substantive overlap among neighbouring bibliometric corpora but should not be read as independent validation of the present cluster boundaries.

sec.title: Document-Level Comparison with a Prior Corpus
sec.p: To test whether the design choices of the present study change the mapped structure, the published search strategy of Zhao et al. [57]—(urban OR city OR metropolis) AND (green space OR green area OR green coverage OR green belt OR park OR green surface) AND (diversity OR biodiversity OR richness OR abundance), up to 31 December 2021—was re-executed in OpenAlex on 13 October 2026, restricted to articles and reviews. The Web of Science record set of [57] is not publicly available; the replica holds the database constant and therefore isolates the effect of retrieval and processing design, but not that of the database. In OpenAlex, the strategy returns 5922 works up to 2021, against 3806 in the Web of Science, reflecting broader coverage and a different search field. Both corpora were compared over 2006–2021 by matching OpenAlex work identifiers.

Of the 1545 documents in the present corpus published in 2006–2021, 863 (55.9%) are also retrieved by the strategy of [57], whereas they represent only 16.6% of the 5201 documents of the replica (Table 11). The overlap depends on the retrieval route: 82.1% of the documents retrieved only through the green-space terms are also in the replica, against 30.4% of those retrieved through the tree, forest, and woodland terms, which account for 80.1% (546 of 682) of the documents absent from [57]. These documents are characterised by urban-forestry vocabulary (forest management, tree species, forest fragment, tree inventory), whereas the documents of the replica absent from the present corpus are characterised by park and protected-area vocabulary (urban park, national park, green area, city park), consistent with the national-park cluster reported in [57]. With the same fixed vocabulary and OpenAlex abstracts in both corpora, the lexical partitions of the two corpora agree only moderately (NMI = 0.382; 0.469 on the shared documents alone), and the partition of the replica is itself unstable, its modal cluster count occurring in only 8% of runs. In contrast, the USA and China rank first and second in both corpora for 2006–2021, so the ranking of China ahead of the USA over the full period (Section 3.4) reflects the publications of 2022–2026 rather than the retrieval design. The urban-forestry terms are therefore what distinguish the present corpus from a green-space mapping of the same field.

sec.title: 4.7. Implications for Urban Biodiversity Research and Conservation Practice
sec.p: The analysis is bibliometric and therefore describes patterns in the literature rather than properties of urban ecosystems. The following observations are consequently framed as hypotheses and research-design implications suggested by the mapped structures, not as ecological findings.

Read as a map of how biodiversity is studied (RQ7), the structures point to three features of the field. First, biodiversity is most often framed through the services, landscapes, and infrastructure it is expected to support rather than as a response variable in its own right. The ecosystem-service and landscape cluster accounts for 41.3% of term volume and the climate, green-infrastructure, planning, and health cluster for a further 24.4% (Table 5), whereas the two clusters defined by organisms—tree and plant species, and parks and faunal communities—together account for 28.8%. Second, the organisms around which the literature is organised are few: trees and other plants (the species cluster and the urban tree and plant diversity front), birds (the parks and faunal cluster and the urban-bird front), pollinators (co-citation community C5 and the pollinator front), and ground beetles and other arthropods (Table 5, Table 8 and Table 9). None of the 17 principal research fronts and none of the six co-citation communities are defined by mammals, bats, or freshwater organisms, and soil organisms appear only in a front on urban soil microbiota framed by human health. Whether these groups are rare in the literature or only dispersed across fronts cannot be established from front labels; a taxon-level coding of the corpus would answer that question.

Third, biodiversity frequently enters the literature through indirect measures. Canopy cover, tree cover, land cover, vegetation cover, and remote sensing are among the member terms of two lexical clusters (Table 5), and remote sensing forms a theme of its own in 2022–2026 (Table 7), whereas species-level approaches appear in the fronts mainly through tree-related microhabitats, biological traits, and acoustic indices of biodiversity (Table 9). Ecological theory is present but concentrated in the co-cited canon: the core rests on biotic homogenisation and on island-biogeographic and habitat theory (community C1), and the woodland-edge front echoes the model of urban assemblages as the outcome of nested filters [11]; these frameworks are, however, rarely foregrounded in the vocabulary of current titles and abstracts (Section 4.5).

These features qualify what this literature can currently support. In the structures mapped here, generalisations about urban biodiversity rest on research organised around a small set of well-studied groups, and much of the applied literature measures vegetation quantity or service provision rather than species diversity. Two consequences follow. Statements about urban biodiversity derived from this field are, in practice, statements about trees, birds, pollinators, and ground-dwelling arthropods; and service- and canopy-based studies, which dominate by volume, contribute to biodiversity knowledge only to the extent that their structural measures are validated against species-level data. The second point is taken up in the recommendations below; the first defines a gap that bibliometric mapping can locate but only primary research can fill.

Carbon-related and service-related terms are separated in the retained lexical network. The carbon terms do not join the ecosystem-service cluster under either of the two closely competing lexical partitions; they attach to the tree and plant species vocabulary or form a small cluster of their own, and the coupling analysis identifies a 130-document front on urban-forest carbon storage. This pattern suggests that carbon accounting is articulated through the inventory vocabulary of species composition and stem measurement rather than through the service vocabulary, even though carbon storage is conventionally classed as a regulating ecosystem service. Whether this lexical position corresponds to shared data, institutions, or management objectives cannot be established from bibliometric structure alone and should be tested with content or field-based analysis.

Island-biogeographic references remain visible in the co-cited core without forming a corresponding lexical cluster. This combination suggests that habitat-patch, area, isolation, and connectivity concepts may function as background theory even when they are not foregrounded in titles and abstracts. That interpretation is plausible but not demonstrated by co-citation alone; targeted content analysis would be needed to establish how explicitly these assumptions are used in contemporary research designs.

Canopy assessment forms a distinct three-term lexical cluster (canopy cover, tree canopy, tree cover) and a theme of the 2022–2026 period without a co-citation community of its own. Its terms are canopy-measurement descriptors rather than a theoretical framework. Because canopy metrics are also used in distributional and health analyses [30,31,32,46], the mapping suggests a useful methodological question: under what conditions can canopy quantity serve as an adequate proxy for habitat quality, biodiversity, or human exposure? The present bibliometric analysis cannot answer that question, but it identifies a point where metric harmonisation and species-level validation would be valuable.
