In this mapping, health-related vocabulary shares a cluster with climate-adaptation and green-infrastructure terms, its 2017–2021 theme is lexically linked backwards to biodiversity conservation (0.250), and the co-cited health community contains work examining relationships between biodiversity or vegetation attributes and psychological or human-health outcomes [38,39,40,41]. This pattern suggests that biodiversity-specific measures enter health-oriented research mainly through the co-cited canon, while current titles and abstracts frame health within climate and planning agendas; it does not establish that health arguments for urban greening generally rely on ecological rather than exposure-based measures. A targeted review of measurement practice would be required to test that proposition.

Three research-design recommendations follow from these patterns, independently of how the hypotheses above are eventually resolved. First, urban tree inventories and carbon assessments that already record species identity can report species-level diversity metrics alongside carbon estimates at negligible additional cost, allowing the two objectives to be analysed jointly rather than in separate literatures. Second, where canopy cover is used as a proxy for habitat or biodiversity, it should be validated against species-level or habitat-quality data for the same area. Third, studies of greenspace and health should state explicitly whether exposure is measured as vegetation quantity or as biodiversity, so that the two exposure concepts identified in the co-cited health canon can be compared across studies.

sec.title: 4.8. Limitations
sec.p: Database and growth normalisation. The corpus derives from a single database; replication against Scopus or the Web of Science is required to establish robustness to coverage. Growth rates are absolute, so part of the 15.89% annual rate may reflect expansion of OpenAlex and of world scientific output; no relative-production series was computed.

Query boundaries and screening. The query omits urban park, urban vegetation, green infrastructure, urban green, city tree, and peri-urban forest unless a record also carries one of the twelve enumerated resource terms. Recall and precision were not benchmarked, no paratext or retraction filter was applied, and the exclusion of query-defining bigrams from the lexical map was not tested against an inclusive alternative. The green-space terms broaden the scope beyond trees and forests: 54.8% of the works reported by the API enter only through them (Section 2.1), and removing them changes the lexical partition substantially (Section 3.6).

Metadata and entity resolution. Journal sources are unresolved for 118 documents (3.1%), affiliation countries are missing for 523 (14.0%), and corresponding-author flags cover 66.3% of the corpus, so country analyses rest on different available-case subsets. Author counts depend on unverified automated disambiguation, and deduplication was title-based rather than DOI-first. Cited records indexed under several OpenAlex identifiers were merged only when their titles were identical and their years at most one year apart, so a work can remain split, as The Theory of Island Biogeography is between two records.

Text and preprocessing. Abstracts are available for 82.6% of documents after supplementation, and missing abstracts are concentrated in two publishers (Section 2.3); the lexical domains are robust to text availability (NMI 0.708–0.872), but the cluster boundaries depend on query scope (Section 3.6). No language filter, language-specific tokenisation, or -ise/-ize harmonisation was applied (7.4% of records are non-English or lack language metadata).

Temporal comparability. The three periods contain 700, 845, and 2202 documents and the last includes the partial year 2026; raw thematic weights are therefore not comparable across periods, and no 2022–2025 sensitivity analysis was performed.

Algorithmic robustness. Louvain rather than Leiden was used, which does not exclude internally disconnected communities [77]. The vocabulary size, tie pruning, collaboration filter, co-citation selection and edge threshold, and coupling threshold (which retains 57.4% of the corpus) were not varied; modularity was judged against the 0.30 heuristic rather than null models; and custom indicators were not cross-validated against an independent implementation.

Interpretive steps. Cluster and front labels were assigned by the authors without an agreement statistic. The Table 10 crosswalk uses a reference set fixed in advance, but inter-coder agreement on its citation-side entries is moderate (Cohen’s κ = 0.44) and rests on 12 coded entries. The strategic diagram relies on a median split across six clusters; four of the six assignments are invariant under a mean/geometric-mean centring.

Materials and software screening. The raw files and scripts of the original extraction of 17 August 2026 were not retained; all reported results were therefore recomputed on the extraction of 13 October 2026, whose scripts, audit values, document-level metadata (without abstracts), and derived tables are provided in Supplementary File S1. Candidate software citations were identified by an over-inclusive automatic screen without manual verification, so a small number of non-software works may have been excluded; the screen affects at most 1.20% of citation links, and excluding all flagged items rather than only the 500 most cited leaves the coupling structure essentially unchanged (Section 2.4).

Relation to prior bibliometrics. No document-level overlap with the corpora of [56,58,59,60] was computed. The comparison with [57] (Section Document-Level Comparison with a Prior Corpus) holds the database constant and therefore does not isolate the effect of the database [65].

Inference. Bibliometric association establishes no causal relationship; interpretations concerning intellectual influence, thematic origin, or research practice require independent content-based evidence.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: This study maps an OpenAlex corpus of 3747 documents published from 2006 to 17 August 2026 and retrieved on 13 October 2026, using a documented retrieval expression, explicit extraction-integrity checks, and deduplication. The corpus is distributed across 1316 journals and 407 publishers. Author affiliations span 124 countries; China has the largest publication count on both reported attribution bases, while Germany and the USA have the highest betweenness in the thresholded collaboration network. Restricted to 2006–2021, the USA leads in publication count (Section Document-Level Comparison with a Prior Corpus). No interpretable community structure is detected in that collaboration network under the stated threshold and modularity heuristic.

The reported six-cluster lexical solution comprises urban biodiversity, ecosystem services, and landscape; climate change, green infrastructure, planning, and health; tree and plant species composition, and carbon; urban parks and faunal communities; urban heat and air quality; and canopy assessment. A seven-cluster solution, in which the carbon terms form a cluster of their own, occurs slightly more often, so the six-cluster partition should not be treated as unique. The domains recur when only abstract-complete documents or only OpenAlex abstracts are used (normalised mutual information 0.708–0.872), but the partition changes substantially when the documents retrieved only through green-space terms are removed (0.404). The top-200 co-citation network yields a six-community solution at Q = 0.507, with an almost identical five-community alternative. Bibliographic coupling at the selected threshold yields seventeen fronts with at least fifteen documents, but the coupling network retains only 57.4% of the corpus. The qualitative crosswalk among the three structures indicates partial thematic overlap, with moderate inter-coder agreement (Cohen’s κ = 0.44); the citation structures are coarser than the lexical domains, and the crosswalk is not evidence of one-to-one correspondence.

Across the complete years 2006–2025, retrieved annual output increased at a compound rate of 15.89%, an absolute value that is not normalised for changing database coverage or overall scientific growth. Publication and authorship are dispersed across many outlets and contributors. In the temporal partitions, ecosystem services, tree species, and plant species persist across all three periods; health vocabulary forms a distinct theme in 2017–2021 and joins the climate-change theme in 2022–2026, heat vocabulary forms a continuous chain, and remote sensing and canopy cover form themes only in 2022–2026. Because that final interval is much larger and contains an incomplete year, these temporal patterns require sensitivity analysis before being interpreted as robust. The co-cited core draws heavily on general ecology and conservation, while the coupling analysis identifies multiple research fronts within the retained reference-similar subnetwork. For biodiversity research, the mapped structures show a field organised mainly around ecosystem services, landscapes, vegetation structure, and a few well-studied groups—trees and other plants, birds, pollinators, and ground-dwelling arthropods—with ecological theory concentrated in the co-cited canon (Section 4.7).

Three practical observations concern bibliometric workflow. First, repeated stochastic runs reveal when a reported Louvain solution competes closely with alternative partitions, information that should accompany community counts together with a description of how the alternatives differ. Second, retrieval integrity should be checked against both returned-row counts and distinct identifiers because rate-limited multi-page extraction can fail without an obvious size discrepancy. Third, software references, duplicate records of the same cited work, and identifiers without metadata can occupy prominent positions in citation data; their treatment should therefore be specified explicitly and, where possible, tested for sensitivity rather than treated as automatic.

Priority robustness analyses are therefore: replication against an independent bibliographic database; an institution-level co-authorship network; a temporal rerun that excludes partial-year 2026; sensitivity analyses for the main network thresholds and for inclusion versus exclusion of query terms; manual verification of candidate software citations; comparison of the author-text lexical domains with an analysis based on the platform’s topic assignments; comparison of Louvain with Leiden and, where feasible, degree-preserving null models; independent cross-validation of custom indicators; quantitative comparison of lexical, co-citation, and coupling partitions; and extension to the pre-2006 literature if the historical emergence of the domain is to be analysed.
